name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER12_MCQ_Q01 - Components and proton gradient of ATP synthase

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents the mechanism of ATP synthesis in the mitochondrion through ATP synthase (Complex V):

Which of the following correctly identifies components A and B, along with their respective functional characteristics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The visual schematic shows the ATP synthase enzyme complex (Complex V) residing in the inner mitochondrial membrane, separating the intermembrane space from the mitochondrial matrix.

Step 2: Structural Identification of Components
Component A is embedded directly within the hydrophobic core of the inner mitochondrial membrane; it represents the \(F_0\) integral membrane protein complex, which functions as a transmembrane channel facilitating proton translocation.
Component B projects outward into the mitochondrial matrix; it represents the \(F_1\) headpiece, a peripheral membrane protein complex that houses the catalytic site responsible for the condensation of ADP and inorganic phosphate (\(\text{P}_i\)) into ATP.

Step 3: Directionality of the Proton Flux and Chemiosmosis
During electron transport, protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical proton gradient. ATP synthesis occurs when protons move down this gradient from the intermembrane space into the mitochondrial matrix through the \(F_0\) channel. According to the textbook, passage of \(4\text{H}^+\) through \(F_0\) couples with the catalytic site on \(F_1\) to generate one molecule of ATP.

Step 4: Evaluation of Physiological Properties
The \(F_0\) portion acts as an integral channel across the inner membrane, while the \(F_1\) portion is a peripheral headpiece facing the matrix where ATP is produced.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Component A is the \(F_0\) integral membrane protein complex serving as the proton channel, and component B is the \(F_1\) peripheral headpiece containing the catalytic site for ATP synthesis in the matrix.

answer.text: A is the \(F_0\) integral membrane protein complex that acts as a transmembrane proton channel; B is the \(F_1\) peripheral headpiece protruding into the matrix that contains the catalytic site for ATP synthesis.
A is the \(F_1\) peripheral membrane protein that hydrolyses ATP; B is the \(F_0\) channel protein embedded in the outer mitochondrial membrane.
A is the \(F_0\) peripheral complex located on the outer side of the inner membrane; B is the \(F_1\) integral channel allowing protons to exit from the matrix to the intermembrane space.
A is an integral protein complex that produces ATP; B is a peripheral protein that pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space against their concentration gradient.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER12_MCQ_Q02 - Pathways and enzymes of anaerobic fermentation

questiontext.text:
Examine the following schematic flowchart depicting the major pathways of anaerobic respiration:

Based on the diagram, which of the following statements correctly identifies the products [P], [Q], and [R], and accurately describes the enzymatic events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The pathway outlines the glycolytic formation of pyruvic acid from glucose, followed by two separate anaerobic pathways originating from pyruvic acid.

Step 2: Identification of Products
Branch X depicts alcoholic fermentation, typically occurring in yeast, where pyruvic acid is converted into ethanol (Product [P]) and carbon dioxide (Gas [Q]).
Branch Y depicts lactic acid fermentation, occurring in certain lactic acid bacteria and fatigued animal muscle cells, yielding lactic acid (Product [R]).

Step 3: Identification of Enzymes and Decarboxylation Steps
The conversion of pyruvic acid to ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\) requires two enzymes: pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. Decarboxylation occurs here, releasing \(\text{CO}_2\).
The conversion of pyruvic acid to lactic acid is catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase. No carbon dioxide is evolved in this reaction because both pyruvic acid and lactic acid are three-carbon molecules.

Step 4: Redox Balance Evaluation
In both branches, \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) synthesised during the oxidation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is reoxidised back to \(\text{NAD}^+\), thereby allowing glycolysis to continue under anaerobic conditions.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Product [P] is ethanol, Gas [Q] is carbon dioxide, Product [R] is lactic acid; decarboxylation occurs exclusively during the synthesis of ethanol, not during lactic acid production.

answer.text: [P] is ethanol, [Q] is \(\text{CO}_2\), and [R] is lactic acid; decarboxylation occurs during the formation of [P], but not during the formation of [R].
[P] is lactic acid, [Q] is \(\text{CO}_2\), and [R] is ethanol; both pathways involve decarboxylation by pyruvate decarboxylase.
[P] is ethanol, [Q] is \(\text{O}_2\), and [R] is acetyl CoA; \(\text{NAD}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) in both branches.
[P] is methanol, [Q] is \(\text{CO}_2\), and [R] is pyruvic acid; net gain of ATP in both pathways combined is 4 ATP per glucose.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER12_MCQ_Q03 - Intermediates and decarboxylation in citric acid cycle

questiontext.text:
The diagram below provides a summary of the Citric Acid Cycle operating in the mitochondrial matrix:

Which option correctly identifies the carbon number and name of Intermediate [X], and states the total number of \(\text{CO}_2\) molecules liberated strictly within one turn of the cyclic pathway (from citric acid back to oxaloacetic acid)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The visual displays the cyclic reactions of the Krebs' cycle (TCA cycle) in the mitochondrial matrix, initiated by the condensation of Acetyl CoA (2C) with Oxaloacetic acid (4C) to yield Citric acid (6C).

Step 2: Identification of Intermediate [X]
Citric acid undergoes isomerisation to isocitrate followed by the first oxidative decarboxylation step, catalysed by isocitrate dehydrogenase, to form \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid. Because one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\) is lost from the 6-carbon citrate molecule, \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid is a 5-carbon compound.

Step 3: Identification of Decarboxylation Events in the Cycle
Within one single turn of the cycle itself (from citrate to the regeneration of oxaloacetate):
1. Conversion of 6C citrate/isocitrate to 5C \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid releases one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\).
2. Conversion of 5C \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid to 4C succinyl-CoA releases a second molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\).
Therefore, exactly two molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are liberated within one turn of the cycle.

Step 4: Distinction from Total Respiration Decarboxylation
The oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA also releases one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\), but that is part of the link reaction (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex), occurring prior to the entry of acetyl CoA into the cycle itself.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Intermediate [X] is \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid containing 5 carbons, and exactly 2 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released per turn of the Citric Acid Cycle.

answer.text: Intermediate [X] is \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid (5 carbons); exactly 2 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released per turn of the cycle.
Intermediate [X] is succinyl-CoA (4 carbons); exactly 3 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released per turn of the cycle.
Intermediate [X] is \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid (5 carbons); exactly 3 molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released per turn of the cycle.
Intermediate [X] is cis-aconitic acid (6 carbons); exactly 1 molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\) is released per turn of the cycle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER12_MCQ_Q04 - Electron carriers and complexes of electron transport system

questiontext.text:
The following schematic illustrates the organization of the electron transport system (ETS) and mobile electron carriers across the inner mitochondrial membrane:

Based on the schematic diagram and established principles of mitochondrial ETS, consider the following statements regarding carriers X and Y and the associated complexes:

  1. Carrier X is ubiquinone, located within the hydrophobic core of the inner membrane, which receives electrons from both Complex I and Complex II.
  2. Carrier Y is cytochrome c, a small peripheral protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane that shuttles electrons between Complex III and Complex IV.
  3. Complex IV contains cytochromes a and a3, along with two copper centres, and passes electrons to molecular oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor.
  4. Unlike Complex I, III, and IV, Complex II does not pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane into the intermembrane space.

Which of the combinations given below contains all correct statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The question presents the architectural arrangement of the respiratory chain (Complexes I to IV) and mobile electron shuttles across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Step 2: Identification of Mobile Carriers X and Y
Carrier X represents ubiquinone (UQ), a lipophilic mobile electron carrier residing entirely within the lipid bilayer of the inner membrane. It receives reducing equivalents from both Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, via \(\text{FADH}_2\)), becoming reduced to ubiquinol (\(\text{UQH}_2\)). Thus, Statement I is scientifically accurate.
Carrier Y represents cytochrome c, a small water-soluble heme protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane (facing the intermembrane space). It acts as a mobile carrier transferring electrons between Complex III (cytochrome \(bc_1\) complex) and Complex IV. Thus, Statement II is scientifically accurate.

Step 3: Characterisation of Complex IV
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) possesses two heme moieties (cytochromes \(a\) and \(a_3\)) and two binuclear copper centres (\(\text{Cu}_A\) and \(\text{Cu}_B\)). It coordinates the four-electron reduction of molecular oxygen to form two molecules of water, with oxygen serving as the final electron/hydrogen acceptor. Thus, Statement III is scientifically accurate.

Step 4: Energetics of Proton Translocation
The free energy released as electrons flow through Complexes I, III, and IV is coupled to the active pumping of protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) operates with a smaller free energy change and does not translocate protons across the membrane. Thus, Statement IV is scientifically accurate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All four statements (I, II, III, and IV) are fully valid and consistent with Class 11 plant respiration physiology.
